Taxing the Sun

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
We are the only people decoding these costs for our viewers.

Summary:
Can you still afford your monthly electricity bill? Electricity is fast becoming a luxury item and everyone is affected.

Maybe you broke the bank and went solar when Eskom was burning through billions in diesel last year and couldn’t keep the lights on. Again. Well guess what? Even solar users will not escape Eskom’s latest proposed charges – if you have put Solar on your roof, beware there is a registration fee payable- and if you don’t cough up, you are in for penalties. You have a year. Now that Eskom has stabilized the grid, and still finds itself owed R97 billion by collapsing municipalities they are needing to raise revenue. And they are coming after you, the budget beaten consumer.


Further information:
They say its to protect the safety of the grid but that isn’t the whole truth. Eskom now wants anything between R2000 and R16 000 to get an engineer to sign off your system. But it doesn’t end there – consumers are being told they may have to pay a structural engineer to ensure that the roof that holds their panels is sound. This after South Africans, desperate for reliable, affordable electricity have put 6000 MW of renewable energy into the economy – equivalent to six stages of loadshedding – and quite literally saved Eskom’s bacon- at their own expense.

But that is not all. Eskom has just received approval from NERSA to change the way it bills customers. It’s about to go onto a TIME OF USE tariff. What that really means is that in some instances the costs of the supply of electricity will go down, in others it will skyrocket. If you have solar you will need a new time of use meter – pay up at your own expense. And still there is more. Apart from a mountain of red tape, delays and paying the costs of an engineer to approve your system, you are also going to have to pay a fixed line cost. This is an additional R200 per month for the benefit of using Eskom’s system which they have to maintain. But you- naughty consumer are now using it like a battery – and Eskom maintain it’s not fair to the other users who pay for its upkeep. They have a point, but still the Solar guys who went into debt to the tune of almost R200 000 for their system – are grumpy about having to find more money to feed into the black hole of Eskom’s finances.

And they are a black hole. In a recent Auditor General report to parliament just 21 days ago, governance, and financial misconduct at Eskom has still not been addressed.
Nine years after we first learned that Eskom had become state capture central, and even as Eskom tries to milk consumers more, their own house is still not in order.

Tangled in a time of use.
You can be forgiven for not understanding how the entire electricity billing landscape is about to undergo a seismic shift. Beyond the basics, few people understand it. To make it worse there is no standard fee- What Eskom may charge for a particular kwh, could be different to the City of Johannesburg’s fee, or any of the other 127 municipalities that all have their own billing system. Time of use really describes the more energy in the system at any given time, the cheaper the power. So conversely peak demand equals higher prices of electricity. What may shock you to know is that the difference in charges in some municipalities can be anything from R1.54 a kilowatt hour to R9.10 per kilowatt hour in winter. An almost 500% difference between the lowest and highest fees.
Eskom wants us to believe that we may be paying less for electricity, but it’s more than likely a sleight of hand, because despite some charges going down – there are fixed costs that you will have no control over, that must be paid, every month. The only way you can escape is to go right off the grid entirely, and few can afford that.

Carte Blanche tries to make sense of the new billing system for Electricity where the only certainty is that you will have to pay more.

Script:


Taxing the Sun Script for voice fact checked.

Audio

Voice over 1
A week ago, the country woke up with a shock.

Eskom! Not again.

We were back in familiar territory. Stage 6 black outs.

By 11 am last Sunday, the electricity minister, the Eskom CEO and the chairperson of the board were apologising to the country.

Mteto Nyati Chairperson of the board, Eskom.
As the board of Eskom we truly apologise for finding ourselves to be where we are right now.

Voice over 2
They promised it would soon be over. By Thursday loadshedding was suspended.

But ahead lies hidden reefs for overburdened electricity consumers.

Power goes up by 12.7% next month. The way residents pay for electricity is about to fundamentally change, and if you installed solar – saving the grid around six stages of loadshedding in total, Eskom and the municipalities are coming after you for more revenue.

Richard Douglas The Green Way Solar
There hasn’t been a lot of thanks to people who installed embedded generation. So, are we taxing the sun? We don’t want onerous charges it needs to be reasonable charges

Voice over 3
Now they want you to register your solar system. Failure to do so, will lead to penalties.

Jenna
Why should there be extra costs, if Eskom can’t give us a reliable power source, we will find alternate ways and now we are being punished for being pro- active and coming up with our own solutions

FADE TO BLACK


Voice over 4
Rein Snoeck Henkermans owns a Pretoria based solar company, and has been tracking the cost of power increases for an average household

Rein Snoeck Henkermans Alumo Energy
800 KW in 2014, 2015, you would have spent just over a R1000 rand give or take. Today if you had to have exactly the same amount of kilowatts in your house, your electricity bill would have tripled, you would have been just shy of R3000 on your bill.

Voice over 5
Incredibly, Eskom wanted us to pay 36 % more from April this year. But the National Energy Regulator, the body that oversees electricity pricing, said no

Rein Snoeck Henkermans Alumo Energy
That would have crippled the country, but they had to give an increase to make sure Eskom is still sustainable. Just remember that 12.74 is the fourth highest increase in the last ten years, so we all relieved, but still astronomically high.

LINK
NERSA as the regulator, has to balance Eskom’s sustainability while being fair to us, the electricity user. But Eskom is in so much debt, its always going to be asking for so much more money but we just don’t have it, so how do you even begin to balance that?

Voice over 6
Brian Sechotlho is the head of electricity pricing and tariffs at Nersa.

Brian Sechotlho
Eskom came to us with 36% and we managed to go as far as 12.7% because we believe that 36% will probably kill the economy.
Masa Kekana
That is quite a delicate spot to be in, because your role is to try and keep Eskom sustainable, and also protect us as the consumer – how do you do both?
Brian
That is why I keep my head shaved, because I don’t want to show my grey hair …
Masa
laughs
Brian Sechotlho
it’s a very difficult one.



Voice over 7
Despite a significant reduction in power cuts, Chris Yelland from tax lobby group, OUTA, says Eskom remains a risk to the country.

Masa
How would you describe Eskom. Does it have its house in order?
Chris Yelland
Most definitely not. Let’s just look at the three main pillars of sustainability.

Voice over 8
And, he maintains, it fails as a sustainable business

Chris Yelland Energy Advisor OUTA
R400 billion rand of debt, that cannot be serviced from revenue after expenses. The municipal arrear debt, topping R100 billion and increasing at a rate of R1.5 billion per month. Operational sustainability, we went for 300 days without loadshedding shows a significant improvement, but we are not out of the woods yet. We know that because we have stage four loadshedding today, as we speak!

Voice over 9
So, Eskom needs revenue desperately, but as high-income customers install solar, and municipalities don’t pay for the electricity provided to them, Eskom’s death spiral is continuing.

Voice over 10
In response, a plan has been hatched to change how we’re charged for our electricity. Under this plan, we’ll be able to choose what’s known as a time of use tariff which means higher fixed costs and savings if our lifestyles change and we run our dishwashers at midnight.

Rein Snoeck Henkermans
You’ve got those peak times, morning and afternoon and they can range there are some tariffs they want to bring in that can go from R1: 20 all the way up to R11:00 rand for that peak time in winter, which is not fair on the end consumer
Masa
That is quite a vast difference?
Rein
It’s a massive difference and I just cannot see how the consumer can afford it nowadays

Voice over 11
Solar users will have no choice but to go onto a time of use tariff, because Eskom wants them to pay a higher fixed cost, to make up for the revenue they are losing from these customers.

Chris Yelland Energy Advisor Outa
Eskom are forcing people with solar and battery energy storage, to go onto a time of use because it has a significant fixed component. In other words, even if you don’t use any electricity, you are paying a fixed component.
Masa
You know when one looks at this time of use option, a lot of people who installed solar feel like they are being targeted?
Chris
Yes. I think they are being targeted. They have been encouraged to install these systems; they have even been incentivized through government tax incentives and now suddenly the rules of the game are being changed

Link
Suddenly they are being hit with expensive registration fees, that many believe are punitive.

Voice over 12
Jenna Brown and her husband forked out R250 000 for their solar system at the height of loadshedding, when they had a young child

Jenna Brown
Trying to have a baby, do bottles, just be safe in your home

Voice over 13
But now they are told if they don’t register their system, they will face penalties

Masa
So, Jenna Eskom will require you now to register, and if you don’t you could be penalized. How does that make you feel?
Jenna
Angry! Its 100% wrong.
Masa
Ja
Jenna
we might as well go completely off the grid and have nothing to do with Eskom.

Voice over 14
Richard Douglas first started his solar company in the UK, and later South Africa. Now he has had to bear the brunt of his client’s anger at the recently announced registration costs



Richard Douglas The Green Way Solar
It does feel like we are using a sledgehammer to crack a hazelnut. You need a professional engineer’s sign off on a small 5 kw installation. You need engineering drawings, some of the things they are asking for are very onerous, and that all adds up.

Voice over 15
There is a pre-approval application, then a final application fee, probably a new meter, service charges…

Richard Douglas
Even for small systems they are asking for a professional engineer’s sign off, we need to prepare single line diagrams. Some people would require a new certificate of compliance…

Voice over 16
In this example, R23 000 is being quoted, including the engineers sign off for registration

Richard Douglas
If you make it difficult to be compliant, people will throw up their hands and say what will it cost me to have additional panels and a big enough battery to get through the night and if that is not enough, I will get a small petrol or diesel generator to tide me over.

Voice over 17
That grid defection is being considered by some of Snoeck Henkermans clients. Meanwhile he’s struggling to find a professional registered engineer for his company.

Masa
Why an engineer for a small-scale solar system?
Rein Snoeck Henkermans
It’s really good to sign off the system by have a professional registered engineer, so if something goes wrong, he has liability and insurance, and PR engineers, there is not an abundance of them around.
Masa
If you are in the industry and you’re battling to find one, what about the ordinary consumer.
Rein
And that is the problem with that. So, the normal consumer is going to find one online and he is going to charge like R20 000 a signature! Which is not fair at all on the end consumer




Voice over 18
And then there’s the elephant in the room: solar systems need to be signed off, but some municipalities like City Power in Joburg can keep applicants waiting for months.

Richard Douglas The Green Way Solar
I believe there should be a threshold, so at a certain size, yes, you do want someone from the utility going out, but there are solar systems that are smaller than a swimming pool heat pump out there, which don’t need a site visit.

Voice over 19
We asked Nersa, why they’re making this process so expensive and difficult?

Masa
Isn’t there a way to make it more seamless where Nersa can step in instead of washing their hands off this?
Brian Sechotlho
Because we are starting this process. We need to find a way to say how can we make the registration easy for both ourselves as Nersa and the customers.
Masa
What happens if you don’t comply? Will they be cut off?
Brian Sechotlho
Then you will be cut off from the grid.
Masa
don’t you think it’s a little harsh while you are going through the teething process to still penalise those who don’t register?
Brian
Once you don’t penalise them, if these not so good quality solar system gets into the grid, it will be too late.

Voice over 20
But as solar users are threatened with penalties, ironically, Eskom hasn’t got its own house in order. An Auditor General’s report to parliament, tabled in January found problems with governance, a lack of accountability, inadequate oversight and ineffective consequence management.

Masa
When does Nersa then say look Eskom, you get your house together, don’t scapegoat the customer?
Brian Sechotlho
You are right, Eskom is not getting its house in order. We within Nersa we are also seeing that. Eskom you need to be more efficient in how you run your power stations. And in this approval we just gave to Eskom, we said its going to be 75%, you need to get your plants up to 75% that is an international benchmark.
Masa
And if they don’t?
Brian Sechotlho
If they don’t obviously, we need to take back the money we give to them for maintenance.

Voice over 22
Eskom had to change our scheduled interview and say they have responded to the issues we’ve raised in various media statements.

So, from April you can choose a time of use tariff, but in the meantime some who invested heavily in solar are thinking of leaving the grid, because the fixed costs are too high. But that is not what Douglas is recommending to his clients just yet

Richard Douglas The Green Way Solar
You can’t say look I am going to generate all my own power, thanks for the infrastructure you have brought to my gate, I don’t need it anymore, but then it rains, like it did for a week nonstop and then suddenly I do need the service from the utility. So, there are going to be fixed charges, that is just an economic reality.

THE END 11 53.



PROMO ONE
Stage 6 Loadshedding, billions in debt, another price hike for power. Eskom is back in the news again
Rein
So, 800 kw in 2014 you would have spent just over a R1000 rand, even if you haven’t changed your behaviour since 2014, your electricity bill would have tripled and be just shy of R3000 on your bill.

PROMO TWO
South Africans who invested big bucks on a grid tied solar system now face a costly registration process or a fine
Jenna
Its 100% wrong. / we might as well go completely off the grid and have nothing to do with Eskom.
Richard
It does feel like we are using a sledgehammer to crack a hazelnut. You need a professional engineer’s sign off on a small 5 kw installation.


PROMO THREE
Eskom asked the regulator for a 36% price hike. Instead NERSA gave them 12.7 %

Masa
When does Nersa then say look Eskom, you get your house in order, don’t scapegoat the customer?
Brian
You are right, Eskom is not getting its house in order. We within Nersa we are also saying that Eskom you need to be more efficient in how you run your power stations. And this approval you need to get your plants up to 75% EAF, that is an international benchmark.

You need a professional engineer’s sign off on a small 5 kw installation. You need engineering drawings, some of the things they are asking for are very onerous, and that all adds up. Voice over 15 There is a pre-approval application, then a final application fee, probably a new meter, service charges… Richard Douglas Even for small systems they are asking for a professional engineer’s sign off, we need to prepare single line diagrams. Some people would require a new certificate of compliance… Voice over 16 In this example, R23 000 is being quoted, including the engineers sign off for registration Richard Douglas If you make it difficult to be compliant, people will throw up their hands and say what will it cost me to have additional panels and a big enough battery to get through the night and if that is not enough, I will get a small petrol or diesel generator to tide me over. Voice over 17 That grid defection is being considered by some of Snoeck Henkermans clients. Meanwhile he’s struggling to find a professional registered engineer for his company. Masa Why an engineer for a small-scale solar system? Rein Snoeck Henkermans It’s really good to sign off the system by have a professional registered engineer, so if something goes wrong, he has liability and insurance, and PR engineers, there is not an abundance of them around. Masa If you are in the industry and you’re battling to find one, what about the ordinary consumer. Rein And that is the problem with that. So, the normal consumer is going to find one online and he is going to charge like R20 000 a signature! Which is not fair at all on the end consumer Voice over 18 And then there’s the elephant in the room: solar systems need to be signed off, but some municipalities like City Power in Joburg can keep applicants waiting for months. Richard Douglas The Green Way Solar I believe there should be a threshold, so at a certain size, yes, you do want someone from the utility going out, but there are solar systems that are smaller than a swimming pool heat pump out there, which don’t need a site visit. Masa Isn’t there a way to make it more seamless where Nersa can step in instead of washing their hands off this? Brian Sechotlho Because we are starting this process. We need to find a way to say how can we make the registration easy for both ourselves as Nersa and the customers. Masa What happens if you don’t comply? Will they be cut off? Brian Sechotlho Then you will be cut off from the grid. Masa don’t you think it’s a little harsh while you are going through the teething process to still penalise those who don’t register? Brian Once you don’t penalise them, if these not so good quality solar system gets into the grid, it will be too late. Voice over 20 But as solar users are threatened with penalties, ironically, Eskom hasn’t got its own house in order. Masa When does Nersa then say look Eskom, you get your house together, don’t scapegoat the customer? Brian Sechotlho You are right, Eskom is not getting its house in order. Brian Sechotlho If they don’t obviously, we need to take back the money we give to them for maintenance. metadata.Summary: Can you still afford your monthly electricity bill? Electricity is fast becoming a luxury item and everyone is affected. Maybe you broke the bank and went solar when Eskom was burning through billions in diesel last year and couldn’t keep the lights on. Again. Well guess what? Even solar users will not escape Eskom’s latest proposed charges – if you have put Solar on your roof, beware there is a registration fee payable- and if you don’t cough up, you are in for penalties. You have a year. Now that Eskom has stabilized the grid, and still finds itself owed R97 billion by collapsing municipalities they are needing to raise revenue. And they are coming after you, the budget beaten consumer.
metadata.Further information: They say its to protect the safety of the grid but that isn’t the whole truth. Eskom now wants anything between R2000 and R16 000 to get an engineer to sign off your system. But it doesn’t end there – consumers are being told they may have to pay a structural engineer to ensure that the roof that holds their panels is sound. This after South Africans, desperate for reliable, affordable electricity have put 6000 MW of renewable energy into the economy – equivalent to six stages of loadshedding – and quite literally saved Eskom’s bacon- at their own expense. But that is not all. Eskom has just received approval from NERSA to change the way it bills customers. It’s about to go onto a TIME OF USE tariff. What that really means is that in some instances the costs of the supply of electricity will go down, in others it will skyrocket. If you have solar you will need a new time of use meter – pay up at your own expense. And still there is more. Apart from a mountain of red tape, delays and paying the costs of an engineer to approve your system, you are also going to have to pay a fixed line cost. This is an additional R200 per month for the benefit of using Eskom’s system which they have to maintain. But you- naughty consumer are now using it like a battery – and Eskom maintain it’s not fair to the other users who pay for its upkeep. They have a point, but still the Solar guys who went into debt to the tune of almost R200 000 for their system – are grumpy about having to find more money to feed into the black hole of Eskom’s finances. And they are a black hole. In a recent Auditor General report to parliament just 21 days ago, governance, and financial misconduct at Eskom has still not been addressed. Nine years after we first learned that Eskom had become state capture central, and even as Eskom tries to milk consumers more, their own house is still not in order. Tangled in a time of use. You can be forgiven for not understanding how the entire electricity billing landscape is about to undergo a seismic shift. Beyond the basics, few people understand it. To make it worse there is no standard fee- What Eskom may charge for a particular kwh, could be different to the City of Johannesburg’s fee, or any of the other 127 municipalities that all have their own billing system. Time of use really describes the more energy in the system at any given time, the cheaper the power. So conversely peak demand equals higher prices of electricity. What may shock you to know is that the difference in charges in some municipalities can be anything from R1.54 a kilowatt hour to R9.10 per kilowatt hour in winter. An almost 500% difference between the lowest and highest fees. Eskom wants us to believe that we may be paying less for electricity, but it’s more than likely a sleight of hand, because despite some charges going down – there are fixed costs that you will have no control over, that must be paid, every month. The only way you can escape is to go right off the grid entirely, and few can afford that. Carte Blanche tries to make sense of the new billing system for Electricity where the only certainty is that you will have to pay more.
